comparison: Both evaluate Ca2+ dependence and kinetics of synchronous dopamine release (C23, C24, C26, C27, C28). OpenEval finds claims well-supported by Figure 1B-D data. Peer reviewers unanimously praised this work as 'convincing' but raised concerns (point 5) about whether extracellular Mg2+ was appropriately adjusted for Ca2+ manipulations, and requested further exploration of Ca2+ effects on asynchronous release (point 2), indicating some uncertainty about experimental controls.

Both address the core finding that Syt-1 is required for synchronous dopamine release (C3, C4, C9, C82). OpenEval finds this strongly supported by carbon fiber amperometry showing complete abolition in cKO mice. Peer reviewers unanimously accepted this as the central contribution, stating it 'convincingly established synaptotagmin-1 as the Ca2+ sensor' with no concerns about data quality.

Both evaluate synaptosome immunostaining data showing Syt-1 localization (C29, C30, C31). OpenEval finds claims supported by differential localization patterns in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-C. Peer reviewers did not question this data, implicitly accepting it as part of the 'convincing evidence' for investigating Syt-1's role.

Both evaluate extracellular recording controls (C35, C36). OpenEval finds claims supported, showing loss of dopamine release is not due to impaired action potential generation. Peer reviewers raised no concerns, suggesting acceptance of these control experiments demonstrating phenotype specificity.

Both evaluate electrical stimulation data (C40, C41). OpenEval finds claims supported by complete abolition of electrically-evoked release in Figure 1—figure supplement 4. Peer reviewers did not question this finding, with the acceptance summary encompassing both optogenetic and electrical stimulation paradigms.

Both evaluate 3D-SIM structural imaging data (C42, C43, C45, C46, C47, C51). OpenEval finds claims supported, showing no major structural defects in cKO mice. Peer reviewers raised no concerns about structural characterization, with acceptance summary noting 'high resolution imaging' as part of convincing evidence.

Both evaluate KCl puffing experiments (C5, C54, C55, C56). OpenEval finds claims supported but notes C56 is speculative about mechanism. Peer reviewers explicitly requested clarification (points 4 and 9) about the nature of KCl-induced release and whether it is calcium-dependent, finding the explanation for why KCl but not ChR2 causes release 'not clear,' indicating significant uncertainty.

Both evaluate DAT blockade experiments revealing asynchronous release (C6, C59-C68). OpenEval finds claims convincingly supported by rigorous quantification in Figure 3A-E. Peer reviewers raised specific concerns (points 2, 6, 7) about discrepancies in dopamine accumulation traces, baseline DA levels appearing at zero, and incomplete characterization of external Ca effects on asynchronous release.

Both evaluate microdialysis data on baseline dopamine levels (C71, C72, C73, C74, C77, C78). OpenEval finds the mild reduction in baseline dopamine despite complete loss of synchronous release well-documented and striking. Peer reviewers questioned statistical significance (point 8), noting significance at only 1 of 3 time points, indicating uncertainty about robustness of in vivo findings.

Both address multiple release modes (C75, C76). OpenEval finds three release modes well-established by combined evidence, though notes C76's mechanistic interpretation is speculative but reasonable. Peer reviewers questioned the overall in vivo findings (C75 relates to microdialysis showing multiple modes), expressing uncertainty about statistical robustness.

Both evaluate claims about spontaneous release (C79, C80, C81). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting C79 is well-supported by literature but inference about dopamine release (C80-C81) cannot be definitively distinguished from alternatives. Peer reviewers explicitly asked (point 1) 'How does Syt-1 deletion affect miniature synaptic responses?' identifying this as an important gap requiring clarification.

Both evaluate speculation about Syt-7's role (C69, C70). OpenEval finds claims supported by citations and appropriately framed as hypothesis requiring future testing. Peer reviewers explicitly asked (point 3) 'Could Syt-7 be the Ca2+ sensor for asynchronous dopamine release?' indicating they view this as speculative and want clarification or additional evidence.

OpenEval evaluates authors' interpretation of findings in context of existing models (C83-C87), finding them appropriately framed as hypotheses. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these interpretive claims.

Both address the main conceptual conclusion about multiple temporal scales of dopamine signaling (C8, C88, C89). OpenEval finds this well-supported by combined experimental evidence. Peer reviewers' uncertainty about microdialysis statistical significance (which supports C89 about in vivo relevance) suggests some reservation about the strength of this broader conclusion.

OpenEval evaluates numerous background statements and literature citations (C1, C2, C10-C22, C32, C34, C37-C39, C44, C52, C53, C58) as appropriately supported. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these background claims.

OpenEval evaluates methodological details and control experiment interpretations (C25, C33, C48-C50, C62) as appropriately supported. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these methodological claims, though peer reviewers did question Ca2+/Mg2+ controls more broadly.
